doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Black audiences and students' interest in jazz
summary: Mancuso blames lack of education and fluff-course attitudes for few black students and audiences, and recalls sharp New York recruits.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Do you find that there’s an interest — oh how do I put this — I’m disappointed when I see hardly any black audience coming out to like blues events and jazz events in Utica.
And it’s like where are they and why don’t they have an interest in this music.

I think it’s a lot of lack of education, I really do. I don’t think they have — they haven’t taken many courses in anything like this, and — because I have black kids come and say man I never heard this kind of music. Because they’re into rap and hip hop, and it’s a faster pace and it’s — and history is a pain in the ass to most of these people. You know they take my course because it says pop. Or before it was jazz-rock foundations. And there’s a sense that these courses are — because if it’s not in their major it’s going to be a gimme course. A course should not be as hard as anything you take in your major. And this should be a fluff course. And then they get to me and half the class is getting an E on all my first tests. And they’re not that hard, and I have the stuff on Angel, we have review quizzes for them, I have review sample questions, and these are the same things that are on the test. They just have terrible study habits. And I don’t mean just the black kids, the white kids. And the black kids, they never heard of who Louis Armstrong was, unless their parents were kind of hip and were big on education. And then there are some really sharp black kids around you know. We’re very white in our department. We get some black kids but — you know in the old days, I’ll tell you something, a couple of my friends, Chuck Domenico and Larry Bynum who was black, and this other guy, they used to go to New York City and they would get us some cream of the crop kids. That’s when Steve Rubufsky was here and his whole crew. I mean they were the sharpest kids I ever had. And those guys, when they left Buffalo State, they stopped sending people out to New York City. And they find that they can make as much money from some of these kids who are deprived or whatever and they get financial help to come to the college, and we’re getting a lot of these kids.
